assessmentSummary.identity: A dynamic straight-elbow hanging exercise in which the athlete moves through a small, controlled scapular range: from the assigned elevated or passive start, the shoulders move down to raise the body slightly, then return under control without elbow flexion or swing. The repeated scapular action distinguishes it from both Dead Hang and Active Hang.
currentCardFindings: The existing source correctly defines a small body lift created through scapular motion with straight elbows and a controlled return.
The card is not a partial pull-up and should stop when elbow flexion appears.
The bottom position must be assigned and tolerated rather than described as a universally safe forced passive end range.
The top is a controlled scapular-depression position, not maximal aggressive retraction or a chest-to-bar attempt.
Physical difficulty exceeds exercise complexity because each repetition moves relative bodyweight through the shoulder girdle while grip remains isometric.
Exercise complexity and physical difficulty are the only core difficulty axes. Coordination, supervision, failure consequence, grip fatigue, and audience readiness remain separate.
Five media links are candidate discoveries only. No exact-match decision, safety review, caption review, reviewer identity, or approval has been recorded.

variantDifficultyCandidates.basis: requires isolating repeated scapular motion under full relative grip load while preventing elbow flexion and swing
stable foot assistance reduces relative bodyweight but retains the same scapular timing and elbow-control solution
band assistance unloads the pull but adds setup, recoil, and changing assistance through the small range
rings add stability and grip-orientation demand while preserving the same dynamic scapular action
added load increases grip and dynamic scapular demand and adds attachment, recovery, and controlled-exit requirements
unilateral suspension and dynamic scapular motion sharply increase limb load, asymmetric trunk control, and failure consequence

proposedLoadProfile.recoveryHours: dose_and_context_dependent; count repetitions and assistance-adjusted exposure with pull-ups, climbing, rope work, rings, carries, and other grip or scapular-depression loading

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the same small range and controlled return repeat without elbow flexion pain swing or grip loss; add repetitions or reduce assistance before adding load

coachCues: Check the anchor and step-down first
Start from the assigned comfortable bottom
Move the shoulders down to lift the body a little
Return through the shoulder blades without dropping
Stop when the arms bend or the body swings
athleteInstructions: Grip the bar securely and keep your arms straight
Start from the shoulder position your coach assigned
Pull your shoulders a little away from your ears so your body rises slightly
Lower back slowly through your shoulders
Do not bend your elbows or kick
Step down before your grip or control changes

programmingDecision.fatigueBudget: count repetitions and assistance-adjusted exposure toward grip, forearm, scapular-depressor, shoulder, and vertical-pull budgets
programmingDecision.logistics: include bar allocation, assistance setup, demonstration of the small range, set time, dismount, coaching correction, and turnover in duration
programmingDecision.substitutionRule: use foot-assisted Scapular Pull-Up or supported straight-arm scapular depression and return for the same dynamic intent; Dead Hang and Active Hang change the task to isometric

athleteSupport.plainLanguagePrompt: Keep your arms straight, move only through your shoulders, rise a little, and lower slowly.
athleteSupport.feedbackPrompt: Could you see or feel a small shoulder-blade movement without bending your elbows or swinging?

limitations: No direct biomechanical or dose-response trial was located for this exact small-range Scapular Pull-Up.
Pull-up kinematics research concerns larger pulling techniques and is adjacent evidence only.
Professional instructions simplify three-dimensional scapular motion into coaching language.
No evidence establishes one mandatory range, universal prerequisite status, or injury-prevention effect.
No candidate media has completed exact-match, full-content, cue-quality, accessibility, or human approval review.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Hang from a secure bar or stable rings with straight elbows. Move only through the shoulder blades: allow the assigned start position, draw the shoulders down to lift the body slightly without bending the elbows, then return under control without swinging.

population.clinicalBoundary: Symptoms, instability, recent surgery, neurologic signs, or rehabilitation restrictions require individualized clinician guidance; this card is not rehabilitation instruction.
population.selectionBoundary: Assistance, dose, supervision, and difficulty caps follow current readiness and workout context, never an exercise-card skill level.

fatigueProfile.cumulativeLoadWarning: Count with pull-ups, climbing, carries, rings, rope, and other grip or scapular work.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Exercise selection requires qualified instruction, appropriate progression, safe equipment and space, and individual physical and psychosocial readiness.

Before Scapular Pull-Up, verify the bar, rings, rack, anchor, clearance, assistance, landing surface, and step-down. Stop for pain or pinching; instability; numbness or tingling; dizziness; a slipping grip; uncontrolled swinging; elbow-position loss; repeated shoulder-position loss; breath distress; or an unsafe dismount.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Training should be individualized and progressed from current readiness and movement competence rather than from a level assigned to an exercise.

Scale Scapular Pull-Up with a lower bar, stable foot contact, a box, an appropriate assistance band, shorter submaximal efforts, longer rest, plain-language cues, a visible stop signal, and direct supervision. Record exercise complexity and physical difficulty; do not label the exercise card beginner, intermediate, advanced, or elite.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The supplied videos are discovery candidates only. Public title and channel metadata were observed, but availability, embed response, exact exercise and variant match, full sequence, cue quality, safety, captions, accessibility, reviewer identity, and approval remain pending until the separate verification step and human review.
The exercise instruction defines Scapular Pull-Ups as straight-arm hanging repetitions in which the shoulder blades move down and the body rises slightly, followed by a controlled return.
Use repeated scapular motion with straight elbows as the identity boundary. If the athlete only holds the top position, the task is Active Hang; if the shoulders remain passive, it is Dead Hang.
The source differentiates scapular movement from elbow flexion and describes a small range rather than a full pull-up.
Classify Scapular Pull-Up by dynamic scapular mode, straight elbows, bottom and top positions, implement, grip, assistance, range, pause, tempo, repetitions, and trunk shape.
The anatomy reference distinguishes scapular depression, elevation, retraction, protraction, and rotation and identifies muscular contributors including the lower trapezius.

Represent the task as scapular depression and controlled return under a fixed overhead hand contact, with grip, shoulder stabilizers, straight-elbow position, and trunk control also modeled. Do not describe scapular motion as a single isolated joint action.

evidence.sourceTitle: Scapula kinematics of pull-up techniques: Avoiding impingement risk with training changes
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
claims: Pull-up techniques produce different three-dimensional humerothoracic, scapulothoracic, and glenohumeral kinematics.

This adjacent study supports specifying grip, shoulder path, and technique and avoiding a universal forced position. It did not test the isolated Scapular Pull-Up, so exact range and injury implications remain unverified.
The exercise requires the athlete to isolate small scapular motion while keeping the arms straight and preventing swing.

Score exercise complexity separately from physical difficulty and derive overall as their maximum. Dynamic scapular control raises complexity above static hangs, while relative bodyweight and grip create substantial physical demand.

evidence.sourceTitle: Comparison of the Effects of Three Hangboard Strength and Endurance Training Programs on Grip Endurance in Sport Climbers
claims: Hanging fatigue changes with grip surface, relative load, time, repetitions, and recovery.

For Scapular Pull-Up, additionally track scapular range, return control, elbow bend, and swing across repetitions. Count the exposure with pull-ups, climbing, rings, rope, carries, and other grip or scapular-loading work.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Safe resistance training requires appropriate equipment, instruction, supervision, and progression matched to readiness.

Require a rated anchor, safe bar height, secure grip, tolerable assigned top and bottom shoulder positions, straight-elbow scapular motion, controlled return, and safe exit. Use foot or band assistance before technique changes.
The exercise instruction uses controlled repetitions and a brief top pause, emphasizing straight arms and a controlled return.
Use low candidate repetition ranges, stop with clean repetitions in reserve, and progress control or assistance before load. No source validates one universal repetition count or range.
The instruction starts in a controlled hang, keeps the arms straight, moves the shoulder blades down to raise the body slightly, pauses, and returns without dropping.
Instructions for Scapular Pull-Up must name the assigned bottom, small scapular action, straight elbows, top quality, controlled return, swing limit, hold endpoint, and safe step-down.

evidence.sourceTitle: Train for the Open With CrossFit Affiliate Programming: Pull-Up
claims: The professional plan separates static Active Hang work from dynamic pull-up technique, supporting distinct exercise and delivery choices.
Use Scapular Pull-Up for dynamic straight-arm scapular control, not as an interchangeable passive hang or full pull-up. Place quality practice before fatigue and budget grip and shoulder exposure.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Training should reflect individual readiness, competence, and progressive development.
Athlete support should show start, small top position, controlled return, straight elbows, assistance, repetitions, safe step-down, and pain, tingling, grip-slip, elbow-bend, or swing stop signals.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Qualified instruction, safe equipment, supervision, and gradual progression are core requirements.

Coach support should include anchor and clearance checks, demonstration of the small range, side observation of elbow and scapular motion, first-to-last repetition comparison, assistance options, cumulative grip-load warning, and station turnover.
Assistance, grip, implement, pause, range, and added load can change the exercise demand while straight-elbow scapular repetitions remain primary.

Foot or band assistance, rings, top pause, unilateral loading, and added weight can become controlled variants. Dead Hang, Active Hang, full Pull-Up, flexed-arm hang, and horizontal scapular row remain separate definitions.

alternateAssessments.name: Foot-Assisted Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Stable foot contact reduces relative load while preserving dynamic straight-arm scapular motion.

alternateAssessments.name: Band-Assisted Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Band assistance reduces bodyweight demand but adds changing assistance, entry, recoil, and exit constraints.

alternateAssessments.name: Ring Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Rings preserve dynamic scapular repetitions while changing grip orientation and equipment stability.

alternateAssessments.name: Paused Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: A top pause changes tempo and time under tension without changing the dynamic scapular exercise identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Weighted Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Added load materially changes physical difficulty, attachment, recovery, and failure consequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Arm Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Unilateral dynamic suspension changes laterality, load per limb, asymmetric trunk control, and failure consequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Dead Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: A passive static shoulder position removes the active dynamic scapular action.

alternateAssessments.name: Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: Holding the active position without repetitions is an isometric exercise with different dose and fatigue behavior.

alternateAssessments.name: Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Dynamic elbow flexion and large body displacement create a full vertical-pull identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Flexed-Arm Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: An elbow-flexed top-position isometric changes joint actions, physical load, fatigue, and stop rules.

alternateAssessments.name: Scapular Inverted Row
alternateAssessments.rationale: Horizontal body orientation and pulling direction change load, joint orientation, base of support, and progression path.
